title: Test Bank · Ch. 1
description: Johns & Saks chapter test bank, Ch. 1 (OB and Management): multiple-choice and true/false items, each key re-checked against the 12th-edition text.

questions.prompt: The most important goal of virtually all organizations is
questions.explanation: **Survival** is a goal of virtually all organizations. Profit and productivity matter, but they serve the broader aim of staying alive and adapting to change.

questions.prompt: Organization survival is often dependent on how well the organization can adapt. Which of the following behaviours on the part of individuals is necessary for the organization to survive?

options.text: Being motivated to join and remain with the organization.
Performing their work in terms of productivity, quality, and service.

questions.explanation: Survival and adaptation need people who join and stay, do their basic work reliably (productivity, quality, service), and are **flexible and innovative**. Every listed behaviour counts, so none can be ruled out.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements best defines an "organization"?

options.text: A social convention for accomplishing individual goals through group effort.
A collection of formally organized social entities.
A social invention for accomplishing common goals through group effort.
A combination of people and physical capital designed to accomplish a common goal.
A group which accomplishes common goals through social interactions and individual effort.

questions.explanation: **Organizations** are social inventions for accomplishing *common* goals through *group* effort. Individual goals and purely physical assets do not define an organization.

questions.prompt: Organizational behaviour is interested in

options.text: the behaviours of individuals and groups in organizations.
the formation of groups in organizations.
the attitudes of individuals and groups in organizations.

questions.explanation: **Organizational behaviour** covers the attitudes and behaviours of individuals and groups, and also how organizations are structured and how their environments affect them. Each listed topic falls within it.

questions.prompt: A large Canadian corporation has recently merged with a French company. Which of the following is least likely to be related to the field of organizational behaviour?

options.text: The impact of different cultural values on the newly merged company.
The adoption of a bilingual communication policy for all announcements in the employee newsletter.
The development of an organizational structure for the newly merged company.
The adoption of a new leadership style and the subsequent resignation of two executives in Canada.
The legal restrictions pertaining to share ownership in the newly merged company.

questions.explanation: OB deals with culture, communication, structure, and leadership. **Legal restrictions on share ownership** are a legal and financial matter, not about people's attitudes and behaviour.

questions.prompt: Management is defined as

options.text: the art of getting things accomplished through others.
the art which prescribes how things get accomplished in organizations.
the art of telling people what to do.
the art of getting people to do what you want.

questions.explanation: **Management** is the art of getting things accomplished in organizations through others. The definition prescribes no particular style, so controlling or ordering people is not part of it.

questions.prompt: Who was the father of scientific management?
questions.explanation: **Frederick Taylor** was the father of scientific management. Fayol and Urwick were classical writers, Weber developed bureaucracy, and Mayo is tied to the Hawthorne studies.

questions.prompt: Scientific Management is the process of

options.text: using research to develop the optimum degree of specialization and standardization of work tasks.
establishing objective criteria for promotion and selection of employees.
developing a strict chain of command.
developing a strict set of rules and regulations.
centralizing power at the top of organizations.

questions.explanation: Taylor's **scientific management** used careful research to find the optimum degree of specialization and standardization of work tasks. Chain of command, rules, and centralization describe Weber's bureaucracy.

questions.prompt: When we say that organizations are social inventions we mean that

options.text: physical assets and implements of technology are irrelevant to organizations.
they must have both people and things to be considered organizations.
the existence of organizations is what differentiates humans from animals.

questions.explanation: Calling organizations **social inventions** means their essential characteristic is the coordinated presence of *people*, not necessarily things. Without members there is no organization, whereas many own very little physical capital.

questions.prompt: The idea of bureaucracy was developed by
questions.explanation: **Max Weber** made the term bureaucracy famous, advocating it as a rational way to manage complex organizations. Taylor is linked to scientific management, and Fayol and Urwick to classical principles.

questions.prompt: The human relations movement was critical of
questions.explanation: The **human relations movement** critiqued classical management and **bureaucracy**. It favoured decentralized control, flexibility, participation, and open communication, which are things the movement advocated, not criticized.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements is false?

options.text: The field of organizational behaviour is concerned with the impact of culture on organizations.
The field of organizational behaviour is concerned with determining the most effective structure for organizations.
"Organizational behaviour" refers to both the behaviour and attitudes of organizational members.
If we can accurately predict organizational behaviour, then we can explain the reason for the behaviour.
The field of organizational behaviour is concerned with both formal and informal groups in organizations.

questions.explanation: Prediction does not guarantee explanation: **accurately predicting behaviour does not mean you can explain why it occurs**. The sun's setting was predicted long before it was explained.

questions.prompt: The contingency approach to management suggests that

options.text: one management style should work for all individuals.
the best management style depends on the size of the organization.
management style depends on the demands of the situation.

questions.explanation: The **contingency approach** holds there is no one best way to manage; the appropriate style depends on the demands of the situation. It is not tied to organization size.

questions.prompt: A Mintzberg managerial role is
questions.explanation: Mintzberg's ten roles include liaison, negotiator, entrepreneur, and monitor, so every listed role counts. They fall into informational, interpersonal, and decisional groups.

questions.prompt: According to Mintzberg, which of the following is an interpersonal role of management?
questions.explanation: The interpersonal roles are **figurehead, leader, and liaison**. Disseminator and spokesperson are informational roles; negotiator and disturbance handler are decisional.

questions.prompt: Victor Lee, the production manager with Alpha Electronics, has lunch with Lisa Alfredo, the marketing manager. The topics of conversation range from personal family matters to issues of concern in their respective departments at Alpha. According to Mintzberg, these managers are performing the role of
questions.explanation: Maintaining horizontal contacts with a colleague in another department is the **liaison role**. Spokesperson sends messages outside the organization, and figurehead is symbolic, not relationship-building.

questions.prompt: Robert Rennie, the Chief Operating Officer of Clearwater Industrial Products, is interviewed by TV reporters about recent allegations that the company has been dumping toxic waste into a stream. According to Mintzberg, Robert is performing the managerial role of:
questions.explanation: Speaking to the press for the organization is the **spokesperson role**, which sends messages into the external environment. A disseminator passes information to people inside the organization.

questions.prompt: Two important managerial tasks are the analysis of problems and taking action to deal with these problems. Analysis is closely related to which goal(s) of the field of organizational behaviour?
questions.explanation: **Prediction and explanation** together make up *analysis*. Management is the action that follows analysis.

questions.prompt: Employee satisfaction is on the decline in which of the following areas?
questions.explanation: Older editions reported falling satisfaction with training, promotion, coworkers, and bonuses. The 12th edition instead stresses rising stress, job insecurity, and well-being concerns.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The 12th-edition chapter no longer reports declining satisfaction with training, promotion, coworkers, and bonuses.

questions.prompt: Which goal of the field of organizational behaviour is most clearly exemplified by the practice of introducing a new pay system?
questions.explanation: Introducing a new pay system is taking action, so it reflects **management**, the third goal. Prediction and explanation are the analysis that comes before it.

questions.prompt: Diversity can be defined in terms of
questions.explanation: Diversity covers race, gender, age, and ethnic background, among other dimensions. The text discusses women, racialized groups, Indigenous Peoples, older workers, and persons with disabilities.

questions.prompt: When we say that the effectiveness of a particular leadership style is contingent upon certain factors we mean that

options.text: the effectiveness of the leadership style depends on what these factors are.
the leadership style will only emerge if these factors are present.
this leadership style is effective in all circumstances.
the leadership style causes these factors to occur.
this leadership style is almost never effective.

questions.explanation: **Contingent** means dependent: the effectiveness of a leadership style *depends on* certain factors. It does not mean the style causes those factors or works everywhere.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is false?

options.text: All organizations have survival as a goal.
Organizational behaviour involves both theory and practice.
Prediction is a more complex process than explanation.

questions.explanation: **Explaining** behaviour is more complex than predicting it, because behaviour can have multiple causes and causes can change over time. The statement that prediction is the more complex process is therefore false.

questions.prompt: Organizational behaviour is concerned with groups because

options.text: informal groups can influence organizational effectiveness.
organizations depend on interaction and coordination among people to accomplish their goals.
much work is performed by formal work groups.
groups can influence new organizational members.

questions.explanation: OB is concerned with groups because organizations depend on interaction and coordination, much work is done in formal teams, and informal groups affect goal achievement. All of these reasons apply.

questions.prompt: Effective management of organizational behaviour

options.text: is predicated on good prediction and explanation of behaviour.
is an example of the managerial task of analysis.
is impossible to achieve since each organizational member is a unique individual.
requires quick and decisive action on the part of management.
was the first or earliest goal of the field of organizational behaviour.

questions.explanation: Effective management of behaviour rests on good **prediction and explanation**, since understanding it is a prerequisite to managing it. Analysis is prediction and explanation, not management itself.

questions.prompt: A social invention for accomplishing goals through group effort is a(n)
questions.explanation: An **organization** is a social invention for accomplishing common goals through group effort. A contingency is a dependency, and a manager is a person within the organization.

questions.prompt: The interventions or technologies for change proposed by the field of organizational behaviour (such as certain forms of supervision and job design) most clearly reflect which goal of the field?
questions.explanation: Interventions such as supervision and job design are about acting on behaviour, which is the **management** goal. Prediction and explanation make up analysis.

questions.prompt: A supervisor is aware that a large proportion of his employees are absent on Fridays. However, he doesn't know why they are absent and he can't figure out what to do about it. Which goal of the field of organizational behaviour has the supervisor achieved?
questions.explanation: Knowing absences cluster on Fridays is **prediction**: anticipating when behaviour occurs. The supervisor lacks explanation (why) and management (what to do).

questions.prompt: If prediction and explanation constitute analysis, then management constitutes
questions.explanation: If prediction and explanation constitute *analysis*, then **management constitutes action**.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements by managers reflects a recognition of contingencies?

options.text: "If my employees work hard, I'm friendly. If not, I crack down."
"We took a real chance building the plant in that location."
"Those engineers should get out into the real world once in a while."
"I always try to treat the union steward with courtesy."

questions.explanation: A contingency is an "if..., then..." dependency. Adjusting friendliness depending on how hard employees work shows the style **depends on the situation**; the other statements are fixed rules or opinions.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT usually a requirement for organizational survival?

options.text: The reliable performance of usual assignments.
The continuing membership of particular, specific individuals in the organization.
The ability to induce persons to join and remain in the organization.
Innovative activities which go beyond member's usual assignments.

questions.explanation: Survival requires people to join and stay, perform reliably, and be flexible and innovative. It does not require the **continued membership of any particular individuals**, because organizations are defined by coordinated people, not specific ones.

questions.prompt: When we say the relationship between job satisfaction and turnover is contingent on the labour market, we mean that

options.text: turnover is wholly determined by the condition of the labour market.
job satisfaction depends on the condition of the labour market.
workers will be less likely to quit their jobs in a strong labour market.
the condition of the labour market influences the extent to which satisfaction predicts turnover.
turnover will result in job dissatisfaction when jobs are plentiful.

questions.explanation: A **contingency** means one factor changes how another operates. The labour market affects *how well* satisfaction predicts turnover; it does not determine turnover entirely.

questions.prompt: Which statement reflects a recognition of contingencies?

options.text: "Our company policies ensure that every employee is treated equitably."
"Our aim is to have the best benefits package in the nation."
"We pay labourers by the hour and machinists with a piece rate system."
"After months of study we finally decided to go with a state-of-the-art management information system."

questions.explanation: Paying labourers hourly but machinists by piece rate **tailors practice to the situation**. The other statements apply one universal approach, goal, or policy.

questions.prompt: When I say that my management style is contingent upon the tasks my employees are performing, I mean that

options.text: my management style affects the tasks they choose to perform.
I treat all employees as equals.
my management style is only effective if certain tasks are performed.
I always use the same management style.
the type of task determines my management style.

questions.explanation: If style is **contingent** on the task, then *the type of task determines the style*. It would not mean using the same style for everyone.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four basic types of managerial activities identified by Luthans, Hodgetts, and Rosenkrantz?
questions.explanation: Luthans and colleagues found four activities: routine communication, traditional management, networking, and human resource management. **Entrepreneuring** is a Mintzberg role, not a Luthans activity.

questions.prompt: Parminder Singh supervises the sheet metal shop at Globetrotter Airlines. One of his employees was late for the second time this week and, in accordance with company policy, Parminder warned him that if he was late again he would be sent home without pay for the day. According to Luthans, Hodgetts, and Rosenkrantz, Parminder is performing which of the following managerial activities?
questions.explanation: Warning and disciplining an employee falls under **human resource management** (motivating, disciplining, staffing, training, conflict). Traditional management is planning, decision making, and controlling.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is one of the most important contingency variables in organizational behaviour?
questions.explanation: **National culture** is one of the most important contingency variables, because leadership, motivation, and communication methods depend on where one is in the world.

questions.prompt: The Hawthorne studies illustrated how

options.text: rest pauses can cause employees to lower their productivity.
fatigue can be avoided by redesigning work.
psychological and social processes affect productivity and work adjustment.
lighting can reduce the quality of employees' work.

questions.explanation: The **Hawthorne studies** began as engineering research on fatigue, rest pauses, and lighting, but they illustrated how psychological and social processes affect productivity and work adjustment.

questions.prompt: A recent study of Canadian employees estimated that the high cost of absenteeism is due to which major workplace stressor?
questions.explanation: The 12th edition names stress and poorly designed jobs as major contributors to absenteeism and no longer ties its cost to work-life conflict in a specific study.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The 12th-edition chapter no longer cites this study linking the cost of absenteeism to work-life conflict.

source.note: Updated to the 12th edition: the text now calls this group racialized people.

questions.prompt: Which of the following represents the fastest growing segment of the Canadian population?
questions.explanation: In Canada, **racialized people** (visible minorities) are the fastest-growing segment of the population. The text uses the updated term.

questions.prompt: It is predicted that by the year 2017, the number of visible minorities in Canada will

options.text: be half of what it was in 2006

questions.explanation: The 12th edition projects that BIPOC groups will make up 30.6 percent of Canada's population by 2031, with two-thirds of new labour force entrants being women, visible minorities, Indigenous Peoples, and persons with disabilities.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The 12th-edition chapter no longer gives a 2017 projection; it now projects BIPOC groups at 30.6 percent of Canadians by 2031.

questions.prompt: In less than a decade, the workforce will be dominated by
questions.explanation: In less than a decade the workforce will be dominated by **people over the age of 40**, helped by the end of mandatory retirement and more people working past 65.

questions.prompt: By the year 2015, 48 percent of Canada's working age population will be between the ages of
questions.explanation: The 12th edition makes the general point that the workforce is aging and will be dominated by people over 40, without this 2015 age-group statistic.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The 12th-edition chapter no longer cites the 2015 statistic about 45-to-64-year-olds.

source.note: Updated to the 12th edition: the text reports that only one-third of workers are engaged.

questions.prompt: It has been reported that

options.text: only one-third of workers are engaged

questions.explanation: Only about **one-third of workers are engaged**, even though engaged workers show more positive attitudes and higher performance.

questions.prompt: What are the major contributors to absenteeism?

options.text: poor leadership and poorly designed jobs

questions.explanation: Absenteeism has no single definitive cause, but increasing **stress levels and poorly designed jobs** are the major contributors named. Leadership and downsizing are not given as the major contributors.

questions.prompt: If an organization wants to improve its flexibility, what should it do?

options.text: train workers on all of its equipment

questions.explanation: Flexibility and innovation foster adaptation to change, and cross-training workers on all equipment is a classic way to build **flexibility**. The 12th edition, however, does not discuss how to achieve it.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The 12th-edition chapter stresses flexibility for adaptation but no longer discusses cross-training workers on equipment.

questions.prompt: Most of Canada's top CEOs believe that their number one priority is
questions.explanation: Most of Canada's top CEOs say **retaining talent** is their number-one priority. Attracting new talent ranks only fourth, behind financial performance and profitability.

questions.prompt: Coastal Pacific Xpress (CPX) has a turnover rate much lower than the industry average. The owners attribute this to

options.text: the way the company hires its employees
the way the company pays its employees
the way the company treats its employees
the way the company motivates its employees
the way the company engages its employees

questions.explanation: A people-first way of treating employees is linked to low turnover, as with the best companies to work for, whose turnover is below the national average. The 12th edition does not mention this company.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The 12th-edition chapter no longer includes the Coastal Pacific Xpress turnover example.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best represents the meaning of evidence-based management?

options.text: a manager designs a program to reduce absenteeism based on a book he read on leadership
a manager designs a program to reduce absenteeism based on a program implemented in another organization
a manager designs a program to reduce absenteeism based on an article he read in the newspaper
a manager designs a program to reduce absenteeism based on his previous experience and intuition
a manager designs a program to reduce absenteeism based on a principle he learned in an OB course

questions.explanation: **Evidence-based management** translates principles from the best scientific evidence into practice. Using a principle learned in OB research fits; a book, a newspaper, another firm's program, or intuition is not systematic evidence.

questions.prompt: Geert Hofstede's research on cross-cultural differences found that

options.text: differences in technical and behavioural requirements depend on where one is in the world
technical and behavioural requirements differ across cultures
technical requirements differ but behavioural requirements are the same across cultures
technical and behavioural requirements are the same across cultures
behavioural requirements differ but technical requirements are the same across cultures

questions.explanation: Hofstede's work shows the **technical requirements** for accomplishing goals are the same across cultures, while the **behavioural requirements** differ.

source.note: Updated to the 12th edition: the text now estimates absenteeism costs at $16.6 billion.

questions.prompt: It has been estimated that the total annual cost of absenteeism in Canada is
questions.explanation: The text estimates the total cost of reported absenteeism in Canada at **$16.6 billion** annually.

questions.prompt: Management and organizational behaviour are two different terms for the same thing.
questions.explanation: **False.** Management is the art of getting things accomplished through others, while organizational behaviour is the study of attitudes and behaviours in organizations. OB provides the foundation for managing.

questions.prompt: The text suggests that, in general, explaining behaviour is a more complex process than predicting behaviour.
questions.explanation: **True.** Explaining is more complicated than predicting because behaviour can have multiple causes, and causes can change over time.

questions.prompt: Organizational behaviour is defined in the text as those employee behaviours that contribute to the achievement of organizational goals.
questions.explanation: **False.** OB is the *attitudes and behaviours* of *individuals and groups* in organizations, not only employee behaviours that serve goals.

questions.prompt: The text defines organizations as socially unstructured units of authority.
questions.explanation: **False.** Organizations are *social inventions* for accomplishing common goals through group effort, not socially unstructured units of authority.

questions.prompt: A family could be an example of an organization, as the term organization is defined in the text.
questions.explanation: **True.** A family is a group of people working together toward common goals, which fits the definition of an organization as a social invention for accomplishing common goals through group effort.

questions.prompt: Organizations across all cultures face the same type of diversity issues as exist in North America.
questions.explanation: **False.** Diversity differs across cultures, so organizations operating abroad must understand how local workforces and customers are diverse and culturally different. Business values are not converging on a North American model.

questions.prompt: When we say that organizational behaviour involves contingencies, we mean that the occurrence of organizational behaviour depends on the presence or absence of other factors.
questions.explanation: **True.** A contingency means one thing *depends on* another, so organizational behaviour depends on the presence or absence of other factors.

questions.prompt: The text argues for a very physical, rather than a social, definition of organizations.
questions.explanation: **False.** The definition is *social*: the essential characteristic is the coordinated presence of people, not necessarily things.

questions.prompt: When the text says that organizations are "social inventions" it means that they are essentially defined by people, not things.
questions.explanation: **True.** Calling organizations **social inventions** means their essential characteristic is the coordinated presence of people, not things.

questions.prompt: According to the text, all viable organizations have goals.
questions.explanation: **True.** Organizations exist to accomplish common goals, and virtually all have survival as a goal.

questions.prompt: The field of organizational behaviour is concerned with the actual behaviour or activities of organizational members but not with their attitudes.
questions.explanation: **False.** OB studies both **attitudes** (such as satisfaction and commitment) and **behaviours** (such as cooperation, conflict, and resignation).

questions.prompt: If a kind of organizational behaviour can be predicted, then we must be able to explain why it occurs.
questions.explanation: **False.** Prediction does not guarantee explanation. Ancient societies predicted the sunset but could not explain it.

questions.prompt: The contingency approach to management focuses on systematic improvement in the quality of an organization's products.
questions.explanation: **False.** The **contingency approach** recognizes that no one way to manage is best; the appropriate style depends on the situation. It is not about improving product quality.

questions.prompt: Canada's top CEOs believe that retaining employees has become their number one priority.
questions.explanation: **True.** Most of Canada's top CEOs say **retaining talent** is their number-one priority.

questions.prompt: When we say that organizations are social inventions, we mean that their existence depends on the presence of specific individuals.
questions.explanation: **False.** Organizations depend on the coordinated presence of people, not on any *specific* individuals, since members can come and go.

questions.prompt: Nonprofit organizations have goals.
questions.explanation: **True.** Non-profit organizations have goals such as saving souls, promoting the arts, helping the needy, or educating people.

questions.prompt: Behaviour in organizations can be effectively and efficiently controlled even if it can't be predicted or understood.
questions.explanation: **False.** If behaviour can be predicted and explained, it can *often* be managed. Managers who act without analysis are looking for a quick fix, which often ends in disaster.

questions.prompt: When we say that rewards should be contingent on the needs of the worker, we mean that workers with different needs may require different rewards.
questions.explanation: **True.** A reward being **contingent** on a worker's needs means workers with different needs may require different rewards.

questions.prompt: The idea of Scientific Management was developed at the Hawthorne works in the 1920s.
questions.explanation: **False.** **Scientific management** was developed by Frederick Taylor and belongs to the classical view. The Hawthorne studies launched the human relations movement.

questions.prompt: The field of organizational behaviour contributes to the prediction and understanding of behaviour, but it leaves the technology of intervening in organizational events to other disciplines.
questions.explanation: **False.** Besides predicting and explaining behaviour, OB's third goal is **management**, which includes proposing interventions such as job design and supervision.

questions.prompt: If the employee turnover of a firm is contingent upon the unemployment rate, it could mean that turnover increases as unemployment decreases.
questions.explanation: **True.** Turnover can be **contingent** on unemployment: when unemployment falls, jobs are plentiful and people are more likely to quit, so turnover rises as unemployment decreases.

questions.prompt: Survival is a goal of virtually all organizations.
questions.explanation: **True.** Virtually all organizations have **survival** as a goal.

questions.prompt: The negotiation of a collective agreement with a union is a good example of the managerial role of disturbance handler.
questions.explanation: **False.** Negotiating a collective agreement with a union is the **negotiator** role. A disturbance handler deals with employee conflicts and threats to resources or turf.

questions.prompt: A manager who presents a new company policy to her employees at a meeting is performing the managerial role of spokesperson.
questions.explanation: **False.** Presenting a new policy to employees is the **disseminator** role, sending information inside the organization. The spokesperson role sends messages to the external environment.

questions.prompt: A manager who decides to commit more money and employees to the development of a potentially lucrative new product is performing the managerial roles of both entrepreneur and resource allocator.
questions.explanation: **True.** Turning an opportunity into a plan is the **entrepreneur** role, and deciding how to deploy money and personnel is the **resource allocator** role.

questions.prompt: According to Luthans, Hodgetts, and Rosenkrantz, if success is defined in terms of moving up the ladder quickly, then successful managers were those who devoted above average effort to networking.
questions.explanation: **True.** Managers promoted quickly did more **networking** (politicking, socializing, making contacts) and less human resource management than average.

questions.prompt: According to Luthans, Hodgetts, and Rosenkrantz, if success is defined in terms of moving up the ladder quickly, then successful managers were those who devoted above average effort to human resource management.
questions.explanation: **False.** Quickly promoted managers did *more* networking and *less* human resource management. Greater HRM effort went with unit effectiveness and employee satisfaction and commitment.

questions.prompt: Kotter found that managers use interpersonal networks to accomplish important organizational agendas.
questions.explanation: **True.** Kotter found successful general managers used networks of key people to implement their agendas, through favours and influence tactics.

questions.prompt: Research by Simon and Isenberg indicates that successful managers almost never rely on intuition.
questions.explanation: **False.** Simon and Isenberg found that experienced managers use **intuition** often (sensing problems, rapid judgments, double-checking analyses). Intuition is not the opposite of rationality.

questions.prompt: A pizza company might define quality in terms of speedy delivery service.
questions.explanation: Quality is judged by what customers value, and speedy delivery could be one such measure for a pizza company. The 12th edition, though, no longer discusses defining quality.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The 12th-edition chapter no longer covers quality as a contemporary management concern, so this pizza example is gone.

questions.prompt: Canadian organizations face more severe labour shortages than organizations in the United States.
questions.explanation: The 12th edition says Canadian organizations will increasingly face severe labour shortages, but it makes no comparison with the United States.
questions.scopeNote: Written for an older edition: The 12th-edition chapter no longer compares Canadian and US labour shortages.

questions.prompt: Canada's top CEOs believe that recruiting employees has become their number one priority.
questions.explanation: **False.** Top CEOs say **retaining** talent is the number-one priority; attracting new talent is only fourth.

questions.prompt: The best companies to work for in Canada have an annual rate of turnover that is lower than the national average and half that of other companies.
questions.explanation: **True.** The best companies to work for in Canada have an annual turnover rate lower than the national average, and half that of some other organizations.

questions.prompt: The best companies to work for also have the best performance.
questions.explanation: **True.** The best companies to work for outperformed a matched group on financial performance and stock returns, so great workplaces make good business sense.

questions.prompt: Most managers today practice evidence-based management
questions.explanation: **False.** The text notes that all too many managers act without analysis, looking for quick fixes. **Evidence-based management** is not yet the norm.

questions.prompt: Evidence-based management involves the use of management intuition.
questions.explanation: **False.** **Evidence-based management** relies on the best scientific evidence rather than personal preference and unsystematic experience, which includes intuition.

questions.prompt: If a manger implements a program to lower employee turnover based on what other companies are doing, he/she is practicing evidence based management.
questions.explanation: **False.** Copying other companies is not **evidence-based management**; that means using principles from the best scientific evidence and research.

questions.prompt: National culture is one of the most important contingency variables in organizational behaviour.
questions.explanation: **True.** **National culture** is one of the most important contingency variables in OB.

questions.prompt: The technical requirements for accomplishing goals are the same across cultures.
questions.explanation: **True.** Technical requirements for accomplishing goals are the same across cultures; only the **behavioural requirements** differ.

questions.prompt: The behavioural requirements for accomplishing goals are the same across cultures.
questions.explanation: **False.** The *behavioural* requirements differ across cultures. Only the technical requirements are the same.

questions.prompt: Effective organizational leaders tend to possess identical personality traits.
questions.explanation: **False.** The personalities of effective leaders vary a fair amount; they do not possess identical traits.

questions.prompt: Nearly all workers prefer stimulating, challenging jobs.
questions.explanation: **False.** Many people prefer **routine jobs**, so not nearly all workers want stimulating, challenging work.

questions.prompt: Managers have a very accurate idea about how much their peers and superiors are paid.
questions.explanation: **False.** Managers are **not well informed** about the pay of their peers and superiors.

questions.prompt: Workers have a very accurate idea about how often they are absent from work.
questions.explanation: **False.** Workers tend to **underestimate** their own absenteeism, so their ideas about it are not very accurate.

questions.prompt: Pay is the best way to motivate most employees and improve job performance.
questions.explanation: **False.** Pay is not always the most effective way to motivate workers and improve performance, so it is not the single best way.

questions.prompt: Explanation and management constitutes action.
questions.explanation: **False.** Prediction and explanation constitute **analysis**; management constitutes **action**.

questions.prompt: A manager who wants to move up in the organization quickly should focus on motivating and developing employees.
questions.explanation: **False.** Quickly moving up depends on **networking** (politicking, socializing, making contacts). Devoting time to motivating and developing people goes with unit effectiveness and employee satisfaction.

questions.prompt: A manager who wants to have employees who are satisfied and committed should focus on interacting with people and informal socializing.
questions.explanation: **False.** Satisfied, committed employees go with managers who devote more effort to **human resource management**. Heavy interaction and socializing characterize managers who move up quickly.
